title: Role of Interfacial Coherency on Creep Behavior of FCC/BCC High-Entropy Alloy Multilayers.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: Sputter-deposited multilayers composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers, e.g., CoCrFeMnNi (FCC) and AlCoCrFeNi (BCC) films
recollection.intervention: Guess: Varied interfacial coherency by changing individual layer thickness (from a few nm to tens of nm) and/or by post-deposition annealing; then conducted constant-load micropillar or macroscale creep tests at elevated temperatures
recollection.structure: Guess: Obtained either semi-coherent or incoherent FCC/BCC interfaces; thinner layers promoted coherent interfaces with misfit dislocations, while thicker layers led to incoherent interfaces and possible phase separation
recollection.mechanism: Guess: Creep resistance governed by the ability of dislocations to transmit across interfaces; coherent interfaces acted as strong barriers causing dislocation pile-up and climb-controlled creep, whereas incoherent interfaces allowed easier transmission leading to higher creep rates
recollection.results: Guess: Creep activation energies 250–300 kJ/mol for coherent stacks versus 150–180 kJ/mol for incoherent stacks; two-order-of-magnitude reduction in steady-state creep rate when layers were <10 nm and interfaces semi-coherent; stress exponent n ≈ 6 for coherent vs n ≈ 4 for incoherent systems

score.note: The recollection partially identifies layer-thickness variation and a coherency transition, but incorrectly adds annealing and elevated-temperature micropillar/macroscale testing. It misplaces misfit dislocations at coherent interfaces and omits the grain-boundary-dominated regime. The mechanism is largely reversed: semicoherent M16 interfaces, not coherent interfaces, most strongly impede glide, with proposed amorphization enabling diffusion/interface slip. All quantitative values and trends are incorrect.
